analysis.one_liner: Replaces income taxes with a flat 20% tax on wages and business income, ending taxes on investments and estates.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee with zero cosponsors and never got a hearing or vote, leaving the existing tax code in place.
analysis.plain_summary: Sen. Arlen Specter's bill would have scrapped the graduated income tax and replaced it with a single 20% rate on wages and business profits, after a large standard deduction. It would tax only "earned income" — paychecks and professional fees — leaving dividends, interest, capital gains, and other investment income untaxed, and it would repeal the estate and gift taxes outright. It would also end public financing of presidential campaigns and repeal the funding mechanism for retired coal miners' health benefits. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households living on investments and inheritances would gain the most: the bill taxes only paychecks and business profits at a flat 20%, so dividends, interest, capital gains, and other investment income would owe nothing, and the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes would disappear entirely. Profitable businesses would pay a 20% rate well below the top corporate rate, deduct the full cost of buildings and equipment immediately, and pay no tax on investment income. Anyone with a modest wage income below the generous standard deduction ($17,500 for couples, plus $5,000 per dependent) would also pay little or nothing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, and large estates

how_it_helps.text: Taxes individuals only on 'earned income' — wages, salaries, and professional fees — so dividends, interest, capital gains, and other returns on wealth would be completely untaxed at the individual level.
Cuts the top rate on wages and business profits from 39.6% to a flat 20%, and repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes outright for deaths and transfers after December 31, 1997.
Lets businesses deduct the full cost of goods, services, and property immediately and excludes investment income from their tax base, leaving a 20% rate on active business income only.

The strongest good-faith case for it: one rate with very few deductions would make filing dramatically simpler, and large inflation-indexed standard deductions ($17,500 joint, $15,000 head of household, $10,000 single, plus $5,000 per dependent) would shield lower-income wage earners.

analysis.who_pays: Households whose income is mostly wages would owe a flat 20% on earnings above the standard deduction, losing the graduated brackets and most deductions and credits in the current code. The bill collects far less revenue than current law — the top rate falls from 39.6% to 20%, investment income goes untaxed, and the estate tax disappears — with no offset anywhere in the bill, leaving larger deficits or future spending cuts. Retired coal miners would lose the dedicated financing for their health benefits, and public financing of presidential campaigns would end.
analysis.who_pays_short: Middle-income wage earners and retired coal miners

drawbacks.text: The tax falls only on paychecks: the bill's definition of 'taxable earned income' covers wages, salaries, and professional fees, so a household living entirely on capital gains, dividends, or interest would owe nothing, while a wage earner with the same income pays 20% above the deduction.
Repealing the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes means the largest inheritances would pass untaxed, and no revenue from these repeals is offset anywhere in the bill.
Repeals the subtitle financing coal industry health benefits, cutting off the funding mechanism for retired miners' health coverage.
Repeals the provisions financing presidential election campaigns, ending the public financing system.

Repeals most of the existing tax code's computation rules and deductions, so filers who now benefit from itemized deductions, credits, and lower brackets beyond the bill's narrow three deductions would lose them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill had real selling points: a single rate, immediate expensing for business investment, generous deductions for dependents and modest earners, and — notably — a denial of business deductions for lobbying and political expenditures. But its core effect was to stop taxing investment income and inheritances entirely while keeping a flat 20% on work, shifting the overall burden of funding the government from wealth onto wages, with no revenue offset and no protection for retired coal miners' health benefits. The simplification argument did not come close to balancing that trade-off.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a hearing or vote, and the bill died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Arlen Specter introduced the Flat Tax Act of 1997 on April 16, 1997 and delivered introductory remarks on the floor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day; no further action of any kind followed.
No senator from either party cosponsored the bill.
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 with the bill still sitting in the Finance Committee, so it died without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody gained anything; the tax code simply stayed as it was. Relative to what the bill would have done, wage earners and retired coal miners were spared a tax system that taxes only paychecks, untaxed investment income, repealed estate taxes, and no miner health benefit funding.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wage earners and coal miners, spared the bill

sides.party_line_note: One Republican sponsored it, no one from either party cosponsored, and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.industry: High earners with investment income and large estates
industries.note: The bill taxes only wages and professional fees at 20%, untaxes dividends, interest, and capital gains, and repeals estate and gift taxes — a sweeping transfer of tax burden away from wealth and onto work.

A 20% rate on active business income below the top corporate rate, immediate deduction of equipment and property costs, and no tax on investment income. The revenue these entities would no longer pay has to come from somewhere else.

industries.industry: Retired coal miners and their health benefit plans
industries.note: The bill repeals the subtitle that finances coal industry health benefits, cutting off the funding stream for retired miners' coverage — an ordinary-workers benefit eliminated as a side effect of the rewrite.
The bill disallows business deductions for lobbying, campaign, and grassroots-pressure expenditures, raising the after-tax cost of influencing government.
